summary: Proanthocyanidins are oligomeric flavonoid polyphenols (condensed tannins) found in plants such as grape seed, pine bark and cranberry, and are sold as antioxidant dietary supplements. Cranberry-derived A-type proanthocyanidins are promoted for urinary-tract-infection prophylaxis, while grape-seed and pine-bark extracts are marketed for vascular/antioxidant support, typically at 100-300 mg/day of a standardised extract. They are NOT FDA-approved drugs and have no FDA prescribing information; clinical evidence is mixed and product standardisation varies. They are generally well tolerated, with occasional GI upset; theoretical additive bleeding risk exists with antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy. Concentrated extracts should be avoided in pregnancy and lactation owing to insufficient safety data. This monograph is based on EMA/SmPC-style and review-literature sources rather than an FDA label.

moa: Proanthocyanidins are polyphenolic antioxidants that scavenge free radicals and may protect endothelium and stabilise collagen/elastin, with reported effects on nitric-oxide-mediated vasodilation. Cranberry A-type proanthocyanidins are proposed to inhibit adhesion of P-fimbriated Escherichia coli to uroepithelial cells, theoretically reducing colonisation and recurrent urinary-tract infection. These mechanisms are largely supported by laboratory data; clinical translation is inconsistent across trials and products.

Active bleeding or concomitant anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy (theoretical bleeding risk)
Use in place of antibiotics for active urinary-tract infection

Signs of bleeding if combined with antithrombotic drugs

preg: There are insufficient data on concentrated proanthocyanidin extracts in pregnancy. Dietary amounts from foods are not a concern, but high-dose supplements should be avoided during pregnancy unless advised by a clinician.
lact: Safety of concentrated extracts during breastfeeding has not been established. Avoid high-dose supplements while breastfeeding unless advised otherwise.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is established and pharmacokinetic data in renal impairment are lacking; use with general caution.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is established; data in liver impairment are limited. Use cautiously and monitor as clinically indicated.

moderate: Anticoagulants (e.g. warfarin, DOACs) - theoretical additive bleeding risk; high-dose cranberry has been reported to affect warfarin response in some cases
Antiplatelet agents - possible additive antiplatelet effect
minor: May modestly affect absorption of some drugs by tannin binding when taken simultaneously
interactions.food: May be taken with food; tannins can bind iron and reduce non-haem iron absorption if taken together
interactions.diagnostics: No characteristic laboratory interference at usual supplement doses

common: Generally well tolerated; mild gastrointestinal upset (nausea, stomach discomfort)
serious: No well-documented serious adverse effects at usual supplement doses
rare: Hypersensitivity reactions to the plant source
Bleeding tendency when combined with antithrombotic drugs (theoretical)
emergency: Allergic reaction with rash, swelling or breathing difficulty (seek urgent care)

monitoring: Symptom response (e.g. recurrence of urinary-tract infections for cranberry products)
Signs of bleeding/bruising if taken with anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs

pearls: NOTE: Proanthocyanidins are NOT FDA-approved drugs and have no FDA prescribing information; this monograph is based on EMA/SmPC-style and review-literature data for a dietary supplement
Cranberry A-type proanthocyanidins may reduce recurrent UTIs by inhibiting E. coli adhesion, but trial evidence is inconsistent and products are not standardised
Do not use cranberry products to treat an active symptomatic UTI - antibiotics are needed
Oligomeric proanthocyanidins have low oral bioavailability, which may limit systemic effects
Possible additive bleeding risk with anticoagulants/antiplatelets; tannins may reduce non-haem iron absorption
missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, then skip it. Do not double up. Missing an occasional dose of this supplement is not harmful.
overdose: There is no specific data on proanthocyanidin overdose and no specific antidote. Toxicity is expected to be low; large ingestions may cause gastrointestinal upset. Manage supportively and seek medical advice; watch for bleeding if combined with antithrombotic drugs.
